action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude a structural, vascular or atypical-parkinsonism cause
action_criteria.rationale: PD is a clinical diagnosis; MRI is normal in PD and excludes vascular lesions, NPH, mass and the midbrain, pontine and putaminal signs of PSP and MSA [Postuma_2015]

action_criteria.rationale: He reports light-headedness on standing while taking tamsulosin and lisinopril; measured orthostatic hypotension would be an autonomic red flag and would shape levodopa titration [Postuma_2015]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Reduced putaminal DAT binding, right 1.08 and left 1.32 (normal >1.50), worse on the right opposite the worse left side, with preserved caudate binding: presynaptic dopaminergic deficit
action_criteria.label: Order a DaTscan (123I-ioflupane SPECT) to separate pure drug-induced parkinsonism from an underlying presynaptic dopaminergic deficit
action_criteria.rationale: Current metoclopramide exposure makes drug-induced parkinsonism a live alternative: the scan is normal in pure drug-induced parkinsonism and abnormal when a degenerative deficit has been unmasked [Marshall_2009]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: REM sleep without atonia in 42% of REM epochs and two arm-flailing episodes with vocalization on video; AHI 5.8/h (mild sleep apnea); PLMI 18/h

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Metoclopramide flagged as a central D2 antagonist that opposes levodopa, with prokinetic options free of central D2 blockade; tamsulosin and lisinopril flagged for the standing blood pressure
action_criteria.label: Review the medication list for dopamine-blocking drugs and drugs that lower standing blood pressure
action_criteria.rationale: Metoclopramide is a current dopamine-receptor blocker, an MDS absolute exclusion while it continues, and tamsulosin may explain his light-headedness on standing; both change management before levodopa [Postuma_2015]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol or other centrally acting D2-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics; if an antipsychotic is needed, use quetiapine or clozapine
Do not start levodopa while metoclopramide remains in the regimen
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in older adults or in any patient with cognitive impairment
required_recommendations: Diagnose Parkinson's disease unmasked by metoclopramide: current D2-blocker exposure is an MDS absolute exclusion while it continues, but the abnormal DaTscan shows a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit that pure drug-induced parkinsonism does not cause, and RBD is not a drug effect; confirm that the parkinsonism persists after withdrawal [Postuma_2015][Marshall_2009]

Stop metoclopramide and manage the gastroparesis without central D2 blockade: domperidone where available after an ECG for the QTc, or short courses of erythromycin, with ondansetron for nausea if needed
Reassess after withdrawal: drug-induced signs can take weeks to months to resolve; the abnormal DaTscan shows an underlying presynaptic deficit that withdrawal will not reverse [Marshall_2009]

Once metoclopramide is stopped, if the parkinsonism persists and limits function, start carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg, half a tablet three times daily with food, increasing over 2 to 4 weeks to one tablet three times daily (300 mg/day levodopa), review the response after 2 to 3 months, and measure lying and standing blood pressure at each step because tamsulosin and lisinopril add to orthostatic falls [NICE_NG71]

Advise bedroom safety for the dream enactment (protect the bed partner, remove sharp objects, pad the bedside); if treatment is needed prefer melatonin, since clonazepam adds sedation and fall risk and can worsen sleep apnea

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizure, encephalopathy or episodic confusion: EEG does not separate PD from drug-induced parkinsonism
No inflammatory, infectious or rapidly progressive feature: CSF has no role in this parkinsonism
No murmur, heart failure or cardiac symptom: an echocardiogram does not inform the parkinsonism
No palpitations or syncope; the light-headedness is postural: rhythm monitoring is not indicated
Formal autonomic testing is not part of the PD work-up; bedside orthostatic measurement suffices

accepted: Parkinson's disease (idiopathic), unmasked or exacerbated by concurrent metoclopramide exposure

differential.key_features: Coexisting contributor: metoclopramide can worsen the signs, but the abnormal asymmetric DaTscan shows a presynaptic deficit that pure drug-induced parkinsonism does not produce, and dream enactment is not a drug effect; persistence after withdrawal confirms
Only scattered punctate periventricular foci (Fazekas 1); asymmetric upper-limb bradykinesia and rigidity, no stepwise course, and an asymmetric presynaptic deficit on DaTscan
No cerebellar signs and no urinary incontinence; light-headedness on standing while on tamsulosin; normal putamina, pons and cerebellar peduncles on MRI
Dream enactment and parkinsonism, but independent in daily activities (MoCA 25/30) with no fluctuations or visual hallucinations: no dementia
Evans index 0.28, callosal angle 112 degrees and proportionate sulci on MRI; no urinary incontinence; upper-limb parkinsonism
Full vertical eye movements, no falls, normal midbrain on MRI
No postural or action tremor; bradykinesia with decrement and rigidity are not features of ET

key_clinical_evidence: Mildly asymmetric, left-predominant bradykinesia with decrement and cogwheel rigidity, hypomimia, hypophonia and micrographia, without rest tremor: parkinsonism by the MDS entry criterion [Postuma_2015]
Metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily for 18 months, started before the 12-month motor history: current D2-blocker exposure is an MDS absolute exclusion while it continues [Postuma_2015]

DaTscan with reduced putaminal binding, right 1.08 and left 1.32 (normal >1.50), opposite the worse left side, with caudate sparing: a presynaptic deficit that pure drug-induced parkinsonism does not cause [Marshall_2009]
Wife-witnessed dream enactment (talking, arm movements, striking her): a prodromal synucleinopathy marker that a D2 blocker does not cause [Berg_2015]
MRI with only scattered punctate periventricular foci and proportionate ventricles (Evans 0.28): no vascular, NPH or atypical-parkinsonism signature
Constipation is not evidence of a prodrome here: gastroparesis and diabetes confound it
Metoclopramide carries an FDA boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia with use beyond 12 weeks

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Metoclopramide can worsen parkinsonism, but the abnormal asymmetric DaTscan shows an underlying presynaptic deficit and dream enactment is not a drug effect: the drug unmasks rather than explains the syndrome
red_herrings.data_point: Metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily for gastroparesis for 18 months
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor toward pure drug-induced parkinsonism and away from a neurodegenerative diagnosis

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: He has no postural or action tremor; ET does not cause bradykinesia with decrement and rigidity

sequence_constraints.reason: Exclude structural and vascular causes on MRI before interpreting a DaTscan [Postuma_2015]

alternatives: Domperidone 10 mg up to three times daily for the shortest possible time, where available, after an ECG
Ondansetron for nausea (5-HT3 antagonist, no dopamine blockade)
contraindications: Metoclopramide with levodopa or a dopamine agonist: contraindicated in the EU product information (mutual antagonism); metoclopramide is also contraindicated in Parkinson's disease.
interactions: Metoclopramide is a central dopamine D2 receptor antagonist: it causes and worsens parkinsonism and opposes levodopa. For gastroparesis use a prokinetic without central D2 blockade, such as domperidone where available after an ECG for the QTc, or short-term erythromycin.

Tamsulosin (alpha-1 blocker) lowers standing blood pressure and adds to the orthostatic fall; levodopa can lower it further. Review the need for each and measure lying and standing blood pressure at each levodopa dose step.
Lisinopril lowers blood pressure and can add to the orthostatic effect of levodopa.
warnings: Metoclopramide: FDA boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia with treatment beyond 12 weeks.
Domperidone: QT prolongation; avoid with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and in cardiac conduction disease.
Erythromycin: QT prolongation and CYP3A4 inhibition; tachyphylaxis limits it to short courses.
Metformin, omeprazole and acetaminophen: no clinically relevant interaction with levodopa.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Harold Jennings is a 70-year-old right-handed man who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by his wife with a chief complaint of progressive difficulty walking and generalized slowness that has been worsening over the past 12 months. His wife first noticed that he was walking more slowly and seemed to shuffle his feet approximately one year ago. She also reports that his facial expressions have become less animated, and his voice has become quieter, to the point where she sometimes has difficulty hearing him during conversation. The patient himself attributes his gait difficulties to his knee arthritis, but acknowledges that the unsteadiness feels different from his prior knee pain. He describes a sensation of being 'off balance,' particularly when turning, and has had two near-falls in the past three months, though no completed falls. He denies any clear tremor in his hands, and his wife confirms she has not noticed shaking at rest. He reports increasing difficulty with fine motor tasks such as buttoning his shirt and using a fork, which he has noticed over the past six months. His handwriting has become smaller, which he initially attributed to age. He has also had worsening constipation over the past two years, gastroparesis with nausea was diagnosed in the same period, and he reports occasional episodes of lightheadedness when standing quickly. His sleep has been disrupted, with his wife reporting that he has begun talking and moving his arms during sleep several times per week, occasionally striking her. He was started on metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily approximately 18 months ago for gastroparesis with nausea, and he feels it has moderately helped his nausea. He denies any exposure to antipsychotic medications or other dopamine-blocking agents aside from metoclopramide. He denies visual hallucinations, cognitive complaints beyond occasional word-finding pauses, and denies any urinary incontinence.

neurological_exam.additional: Glabellar reflex positive (Myerson sign — fails to habituate after 10 taps). No myoclonus. No rest tremor elicited with distraction maneuvers (mental subtraction). Mild seborrheic dermatitis noted on forehead and nasolabial folds.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing intact. No dysdiadochokinesia beyond that attributable to bradykinesia. No cerebellar ataxia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal round and reactive to light, 3mm bilaterally. Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. Facial sensation intact to light touch bilaterally. Mild facial hypomimia noted — reduced blink rate and decreased spontaneous facial expression. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait mildly narrow-based with reduced arm swing bilaterally, slightly more reduced on the left. Stride length mildly shortened. Mild difficulty with tandem walking. Two to three steps on pull test before correcting (mildly impaired postural reflexes). No festination. No freezing. Able to rise from chair without using arms, but slowly.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score 25/30, losing points on trail-making (1), letter fluency (1), abstraction (1) and delayed recall (2). Speech is mildly hypophonic but fluent with intact comprehension and repetition. No aphasia, neglect, or apraxia noted.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Mild bilateral cogwheel rigidity at the wrists, slightly more prominent on the left than the right. Subtle bradykinesia on rapid alternating movements bilaterally, with mild decrement in amplitude and speed during finger tapping, more noticeable on the left. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No drift on pronator testing. No action or intention tremor. No clear resting tremor observed during the examination.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, and proprioception intact throughout. Vibration sense mildly diminished at bilateral great toes, consistent with peripheral neuropathy. Romberg test negative.
